verses.confNote: Reconstructed from auto-captions, so the wording is approximate. The sense is clear.

lines.dev: यद्यपि सर्वत्र भारतवर्षे अस्माभिः सर्वदा गीर्वाणभाषया व्यवहारादिकं कर्तव्यम्
lines.iast: yadyapi sarvatra bhāratavarṣe asmābhiḥ sarvadā gīrvāṇabhāṣayā vyavahārādikaṁ kartavyam

words.m: by the language of the gods (Sanskrit)
words.n: gīrvāṇa = 'god', literally one whose speech is praised. A traditional name for Sanskrit is 'language of the gods'.

lines.dev: तस्मात् अहम् इदानीं वाग्व्यापारं म्लेच्छभाषया करोमि
lines.iast: tasmāt aham idānīṁ vāgvyāpāraṁ mlecchabhāṣayā karomi

words.m: the work of speech, i.e. speaking
words.r: vāc ← √vac (to speak); vyāpāra ← vi + ā + √pṛ (to be engaged)

words.n: Traditionally the word for a non-Sanskrit speaker. He says it about himself and English, with humility.
-tvā is the 'having…' ending that links two actions.

verses.meaning: Everywhere in Bharat we ought to conduct our dealings in the language of the gods. But, with time, that is no longer so. Therefore I will now speak in a foreign tongue, begging your pardon.
verses.why: He opens with reverence for Sanskrit and humility about English. The apology also sets his theme: something precious has slipped out of daily life, and he wants us to notice what we lost.

verses.short: Those who give their lives to the Veda
verses.confNote: I could not match this verse to any source online. Only the clearly heard words are decoded.

words.n: Veda is literally 'knowledge'. Related English words: wit, wise, video.

verses.meaning: Most meritorious and greatly fortunate, like Śiva himself, are those who [give their lives to the Veda]. The rest of the line is unclear in the recording.
verses.why: He honours the people who dedicate their whole lives to Vedic study, and then says: that cannot be everyone, but a basic grounding in the Shastras should be for all.

verses.short: Learn conduct from the foremost teachers
verses.confNote: Matches the standard text. Social readings of this verse are debated; here we look at its language and how he uses it.

words.n: Becomes 'etad' before the voiced 'd' of deśa.

words.m: of the foremost-born (the eldest, the leading teacher)

lines.dev: स्वं स्वं चरित्रं शिक्षेरन् पृथिव्यां सर्वमानवाः
lines.iast: svaṁ svaṁ caritraṁ śikṣeran pṛthivyāṁ sarvamānavāḥ

words.r: √śikṣ, the 'wish to be able' form of √śak (to be able)
words.n: To learn = to wish to become able. Third person plural, 'would/should'.

sandhi.rule: A final t turns into d before a voiced sound.
The same: t becomes d before a vowel.

verses.meaning: From the foremost teachers born in this land, let all people on earth learn their own conduct.
verses.why: He uses it to say the Shastras are not parochial. The learning is for every person on earth, which is why he calls their study 'non-negotiable'.

verses.short: Words get power in relation to each other
verses.source: Not identified (the idea is anvitābhidhāna, from Mīmāṃsā)
verses.confNote: Exact wording not matched to any source. The idea behind it is a real doctrine of Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā.

words.n: The 'śakti' of a word is its power to point to a meaning.

sandhi.rule: a + a join into a long ā.

verses.meaning: In all words lies the power [to express] their own meaning. A word in the recording between 'words' and 'meaning' is unclear, so I leave it out.
verses.why: He says: if I tell you this in Sanskrit, you call it scripture; if I say each token's embedding is a mix of the others, you call it great technology. The idea that words gain meaning from their neighbours is old (anvitābhidhāna). It is a resemblance with Transformers, not a proof.

verses.short: Science as a by-product, like straw in farming
verses.confNote: Could not be matched to any source. Only the clearly heard words are decoded.

words.n: He translates it as 'weed'. The Sanskrit word means straw, but his point is the same: a by-product of the crop.

sandhi.rule: a + a join into a long ā.

verses.meaning: [Even if some of it] is obtainable, it is no fruit of this; like the straw in farming. (The middle of the verse is unclear in the recording.)
verses.why: His warning: don't go searching for modern science in the Shastras. Whatever science turns up is a by-product, like straw from a crop. You plant for the grain, which is the real aim.

verses.short: Help others is merit, harm is sin
verses.confNote: A famous verse; the wording is standard. Attribution to a particular text varies.

sandhi.rule: a + a join into a long ā.
t becomes d before a vowel.

verses.meaning: In half a verse I will say what crores of books have said: helping others brings merit; hurting others brings sin.
verses.why: AI is a force we do not know how to handle. This verse says the test of any tool is simple: does it help or harm? So build every algorithm to help.

verses.short: Mukti: standing in one's own nature

sandhi.rule: A visarga becomes r before a voiced sound.
ā + a join into a long ā.

verses.meaning: Liberation is giving up the other forms and being established in one's own form.
verses.why: Today's world says: take everything you can from nature. The scriptures say the opposite: let go of what is not you. Happiness is internal, so there's no need to exploit nature to find it.

verses.short: No hope of immortality through wealth

words.n: A-mṛta is 'not-dead'. English cousins: mortal, murder, even Greek ambrosia.

sandhi.rule: a + ā join into a long ā.

verses.meaning: But there is no hope of immortality through wealth.
verses.why: Yājñavalkya tells his wife wealth can make her comfortable, but not deathless. That's the pivot of the whole talk: the real ambition is something wealth cannot buy.

verses.short: What shall I do with what won't make me immortal?

lines.dev: येनाहं नामृता स्यां किमहं तेन कुर्याम्
lines.iast: yenāhaṁ nāmṛtā syāṁ kim ahaṁ tena kuryām

sandhi.rule: a + a join into a long ā.
a + a join into a long ā.

verses.meaning: What shall I do with that by which I would not become immortal?
verses.why: He calls this the most beautiful line he has ever read. It is a complete test for every goal in life: will this carry me beyond death? If not, why chase it?

verses.short: All life is short; keep your chariots, song and dance
verses.confNote: Matches the standard text. The speaker quotes only the second half.

words.n: English cousins: quick (as in 'the quick and the dead'), vivid.

verses.meaning: Even a whole life is short indeed. Keep your chariots, your dance and song.
verses.why: Nachiketa refuses Yama's offers. The speaker, a mathematician, adds: even if you give me a billion years, it ends, and whatever ends is not what I want.

lines.iast: śeṣāḥ sthāvaram icchanti kim āścaryam ataḥ param

words.r: traditionally explained from ā + √car (to move, behave)

sandhi.rule: i turns into y before a different vowel.
i + i join into a long ī.
a + ā join into a long ā.

verses.meaning: Day after day, beings go to Yama's abode, yet those who remain wish to be permanent. What is a greater wonder than this?
verses.why: Yudhiṣṭhira's answer to the Yaksha. The speaker's point: we do everything in life as if we will stay forever, and the Shastras exist to wake us from that assumption.

verses.confNote: Heavily garbled in the captions and not matched to any source. Only a few words are decoded.

lines.dev: महता भाग्येन ईदृशाः पुरुषाः अद्यापि सन्ति
lines.iast: mahatā bhāgyena īdṛśāḥ puruṣāḥ adyāpi santi

verses.meaning: By great fortune, such people still exist even today. (This is my best guess at the sense; the words are unclear in the recording.)
verses.why: Near the end he says the real question is why we are not studying the scriptures, and he thanks those who keep the tradition alive.

words.r: kṛṣṇa, traditionally linked to √kṛṣ (to draw, attract)
√ṛ (to go), 'to make go to' = to offer

sandhi.rule: a + a join into a long ā.
Written together as one word in the traditional form.

verses.meaning: Let this be an offering to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
verses.why: He dedicates what he said to his Gurus and to Krishna. Study is an offering and a gift, not a possession.

terms.meaning: the science of logic and reasoning

parts.r: ni + √i (to go, lead): that which leads the mind to a conclusion

parts.m: a treatise, a body of teaching

terms.why: The auto-captions said 'jurisprudence'. He means Nyāya, the logic tradition. He says 12 years of it prepares the mind for any hard subject.
What he says Shastra study gives: not facts, but a clear, sharp mind. 'Buddha' comes from the same root as buddhi: the awakened one.
He says today's world has lost this. People are unhappy because success is measured by producing and consuming more.
His name for the biggest ambition a person can have: to be happy for eternity. The same root gave us 'mukti' in V7.
He says asking for instant proof of things beyond the senses is like asking a physicist to prove quantum entanglement in five minutes. It takes years of preparation first.

terms.meaning: that which holds; duty, right order
terms.why: He warns about powerful tools in the hands of someone with no background of Dharma and Shastra.

roots.en: quick (as in 'the quick and the dead'), vivid

quiz.q: What is the 'having done' ending seen in hitvā and yācitvā?
quiz.e: -tvā joins two actions: 'having abandoned' (hitvā), 'having begged' (yācitvā). Don't mix it up with -tva, which makes 'state of' (amṛta-tva).
√muc means 'to release'. Mukti is release; mumukṣā is the wish for release.

quiz.q: In V7, what is 'mukti' according to the Bhāgavata?
quiz.e: Hitvā anyathā-rūpaṁ svarūpeṇa vyavasthitiḥ: give up the other forms, and be established in your own.
a (not) + mṛta (dead, from √mṛ) + tva (state of) = the state of not-dying.

quiz.q: Which sandhi rule makes na + amṛtā into nāmṛtā?
quiz.e: Two short a's merge into a long ā.

quiz.q: In the Yakṣa-praśna, what is the greatest wonder?
o: That beings die daily, yet the rest wish to live forever
quiz.e: Ahany ahani bhūtāni… we see death daily and still live as if permanent.

quiz.q: What does he say about finding science in the Shastras?
o: It is a by-product, like straw in farming
quiz.e: He says don't go looking for science there; if you find some, it's a by-product.

quiz.q: Who asked 'yenāhaṁ nāmṛtā syāṁ kim ahaṁ tena kuryām'?
quiz.e: Maitreyī, wife of Yājñavalkya. The speaker says 'Gārgī', but the line is Maitreyī's (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.4.3).

quiz.q: What does śikṣ (to learn) literally mean?
quiz.e: √śikṣ is the 'wishing' form of √śak (to be able). To learn is to wish to become able.

quiz.q: What is the biggest ambition, according to the talk?
quiz.e: Mumukṣā: the desire for liberation. Everything else ends in death.
